claim: The attentional blink reflects a ubiquitous bottleneck with selecting and processing the second of two targets that occur in close temporal proximity.
source: The attentional blink reflects a ubiquitous bottleneck with selecting and processing the second of two targets that occur in close temporal proximity.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about the attentional blink phenomenon, supported by established scientific knowledge and the study's premise.

claim: The attentional blink impairs specifically one component of attention – sensitivity – while leaving the other component – bias – unaffected.
source: We find that the attentional blink impairs specifically one component of attention – sensitivity – while leaving the other component – bias – unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the signal detection model analysis showing d' deficits but no criterion changes.

claim: Parieto-occipital N2p and P3 potential amplitudes characterized target detection deficits.
source: Parieto-occipital N2p and P3 potential amplitudes characterized target detection deficits, whereas long-range high-beta band (20–30 Hz) coherence between frontoparietal electrodes signaled target discrimination deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data showing correlations between ERP amplitudes and detection sensitivity.

claim: Long-range high-beta band (20–30 Hz) coherence between frontoparietal electrodes signaled target discrimination deficits.
source: Parieto-occipital N2p and P3 potential amplitudes characterized target detection deficits, whereas long-range high-beta band (20–30 Hz) coherence between frontoparietal electrodes signaled target discrimination deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG coherence analysis showing correlations with discrimination sensitivity.

claim: Detection and discrimination deficits were encoded along separable neural dimensions.
source: The analysis revealed that detection and discrimination deficits were encoded along separable neural dimensions, whose configural distances robustly correlated with the neural markers of each.
evidence: This claim is supported by representational geometry analysis showing distinct neural dimensions for detection and discrimination.

claim: Attention is a remarkable cognitive capacity that enables us to process relevant information and filter out irrelevant information to guide behavior.
source: Attention is a remarkable cognitive capacity that enables us to process relevant information and filter out irrelevant information to guide behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about attention supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Attention is surprisingly capacity limited (Desimone and Duncan, 1995).
source: Yet, attention is surprisingly capacity limited (Desimone and Duncan, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: This limitation is clearly revealed when we seek to perform multiple tasks simultaneously or to tackle multiple goals in rapid succession (Kanwisher and Potter, 1990).
source: This limitation is clearly revealed when we seek to perform multiple tasks simultaneously or to tackle multiple goals in rapid succession (Kanwisher and Potter, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When multiple targets are presented sequentially – in a rapid serial visual stream – individuals are often unable to accurately detect and identify the second of two targets, particularly when it is presented in close temporal proximity (200–500ms) to the first (Raymond et al., 1992).
source: When multiple targets are presented sequentially – in a rapid serial visual stream – individuals are often unable to accurately detect and identify the second of two targets, particularly when it is presented in close temporal proximity (200–500ms) to the first (Raymond et al., 1992; Figure 1, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The inability to process the second target has been hypothesized to arise from an inherent delay in reallocating attention from the first target (T1) to the second target (T2) (Nieuwenstein et al., 2009; Vul et al., 2008).
source: The inability to process the second target has been hypothesized to arise from various factors, including an inherent delay in reallocating attention from the first target (T1) to the second target (T2) (Nieuwenstein et al., 2009; Vul et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The inability to process the second target has been hypothesized to arise from a transient bottleneck in working memory while processing the first target (Shapiro et al., 1994; Shapiro et al., 1997; Martens et al., 2002; Chun and Potter, 1995; Potter et al., 2005).
source: a transient bottleneck in working memory while processing the first target (Shapiro et al., 1994; Shapiro et al., 1997; Martens et al., 2002; Chun and Potter, 1995; Potter et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The inability to process the second target has been hypothesized to arise from an inevitable consequence of suppressing distractors that follow the first target in the visual stream (Di Lollo et al., 2005; Nieuwenstein and Potter, 2006; Kawahara et al., 2006).
source: or an inevitable consequence of suppressing distractors that follow the first target in the visual stream (Di Lollo et al., 2005; Nieuwenstein and Potter, 2006; Kawahara et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Previous studies have investigated the stage at which attentional blink affects T2's processing (early or late; Zivony et al., 2018; Vogel et al., 1998; Nieuwenstein et al., 2005; Jolicoeur and Dell'Acqua, 1998).
source: In particular, previous studies have investigated the stage at which attentional blink affects T2's processing (early or late; Zivony et al., 2018; Vogel et al., 1998; Nieuwenstein et al., 2005; Jolicoeur and Dell'Acqua, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have investigated the neural basis of the attentional blink effect, including the specific brain regions involved (Vogel et al., 1998; Dell'Acqua et al., 2006; Luck et al., 1996; Sergent et al., 2005).
source: and the neural basis of this effect, including the specific brain regions involved (Vogel et al., 1998; Dell'Acqua et al., 2006; Luck et al., 1996; Sergent et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several theoretical frameworks characterize a sequence of phases of the attentional blink, including target selection based on relevance, detection, feature processing, and encoding into working memory (Chun and Potter, 1995; Eimer, 2014).
source: Several theoretical frameworks characterize a sequence of phases of the attentional blink, including target selection based on relevance, detection, feature processing, and encoding into working memory (Chun and Potter, 1995; Eimer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: There is little support for attentional blink deficits at an early, sensory encoding stage (Zivony et al., 2018).
source: Overall, there is little support for attentional blink deficits at an early, sensory encoding (Zivony et al., 2018) stage
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The vast majority of literature suggests that T2's processing is affected at a late stage (Martens et al., 2002; Potter et al., 2005).

claim: Scalp EEG studies have reported partial or complete suppression of late event-related potential (ERP) components, particularly those linked to attentional engagement (P2, N2, N2pc, or VAN; Vogel et al., 1998; Dellert et al., 2022; Eiserbeck et al., 2024; Lasaponara et al., 2015; Vogel and Luck, 2002).
source: Consistent with these behavioral results, scalp electroencephalography (EEG) studies have reported partial or complete suppression of late event-related potential (ERP) components, particularly those linked to attentional engagement (P2, N2, N2pc, or VAN; Vogel et al., 1998; Dellert et al., 2022; Eiserbeck et al., 2024; Lasaponara et al., 2015; Vogel and Luck, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous EEG studies.

claim: Scalp EEG studies have reported partial or complete suppression of late ERP components linked to working memory (P3; Sergent et al., 2005; Dell'Acqua et al., 2015; Chennu et al., 2009; Meijs et al., 2018; Kranczioch et al., 2003; Kranczioch et al., 2007).
source: working memory (P3; Sergent et al., 2005; Dell'Acqua et al., 2015; Chennu et al., 2009; Meijs et al., 2018; Kranczioch et al., 2003; Kranczioch et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous EEG studies.

claim: Scalp EEG studies have reported partial or complete suppression of late ERP components linked to semantic processing (N400; Batterink et al., 2012).

claim: Early sensory components (P1/N1) are virtually unaffected by the attentional blink (Sergent et al., 2005; Lasaponara et al., 2015).
source: early sensory components (P1/N1) are virtually unaffected (Sergent et al., 2005; Lasaponara et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Late effects of the attentional blink are hypothesized to be mediated by diverse functional regions within a frontoparietal network, both based on correlational and causal evidence (Marois et al., 2000; Cooper et al., 2004; Kihara et al., 2007).
source: These 'late' effects are hypothesized to be mediated by diverse functional regions within a frontoparietal network, both based on correlational and causal evidence (Marois et al., 2000; Cooper et al., 2004; Kihara et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity in the parietal, lateral prefrontal, and anterior cingulate cortex, as measured with fMRI, was shown to decrease when T2 was not detected (missed), even though stimulus-evoked activity in early visual areas (e.g. V1) was relatively intact (Williams et al., 2008).
source: Activity in the parietal, lateral prefrontal, and anterior cingulate cortex, as measured with functional MRI (fMRI), was shown to decrease when T2 was not detected (missed), even though stimulus-evoked activity in early visual areas (e.g. V1) was relatively intact (Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous fMRI study.

claim: Long-range synchronization of EEG oscillations across fronto-parietal regions in the beta-band (13–18 Hz) is impaired during the attentional blink (Gross et al., 2004).
source: Long-range synchronization of EEG oscillations across fronto-parietal regions in the beta-band (13–18 Hz) is impaired during the attentional blink (Gross et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Converging evidence from transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies suggests a potential role for the posterior parietal cortex in the attentional blink (Cooper et al., 2004; Kihara et al., 2007).
source: In addition, converging evidence from transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies suggests a potential role for the posterior parietal cortex in the attentional blink (Cooper et al., 2004; Kihara et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to TMS studies.

claim: T2 detection and identification performance were enhanced after the application of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the bilateral parietal cortex.
source: T2 detection and identification performance were enhanced after the application of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the bilateral parietal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the cited TMS studies.

claim: Many previous studies have studied the attentional blink as a unitary phenomenon.
source: Despite this extensive literature, many previous studies have studied the attentional blink as a unitary phenomenon.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous literature based on the authors' review.

claim: Signal detection theory is a widely applied psychophysical framework whose parameters – sensitivity (d') and bias (or criterion, c) – quantify perceptual and decisional components, respectively.
source: Signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966) is a widely applied psychophysical framework whose parameters – sensitivity (d') and bias (or criterion, c) – quantify these perceptual and decisional components, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citation.

claim: A change in either sensitivity or criterion can produce a change in the proportion of correct responses (Luo and Maunsell, 2015; Sridharan et al., 2017).
source: Distinguishing between sensitivity and criterion effects is crucial because a change in either of these parameters can produce a change in the proportion of correct responses (Luo and Maunsell, 2015; Sridharan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Whether the attentional blink induces primarily d' deficits, primarily bias deficits, or a mixture of both is largely unknown.
source: Yet, whether the attentional blink induces primarily d' deficits, primarily bias deficits, or a mixture of both is largely unknown, and the limited evidence available is controversial (Lasaponara et al., 2015; Caetta and Gorea, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the literature review and citations.

claim: Previous studies typically employed simple target detection or identification tasks, in conjunction with conventional, one-dimensional signal detection models (Lasaponara et al., 2015; Caetta and Gorea, 2010).
source: This is perhaps because previous studies typically employed simple target detection or identification tasks, in conjunction with conventional, one-dimensional signal detection models (Lasaponara et al., 2015; Caetta and Gorea, 2010).

claim: Simple tasks and conventional one-dimensional signal detection models do not suffice to reliably distinguish between sensitivity and bias components of attention (DeCarlo, 2012; Sridharan et al., 2014; Hautus et al., 2021).
source: Recent literature suggests that such tasks and models do not suffice to reliably distinguish between sensitivity and bias components of attention (DeCarlo, 2012; Sridharan et al., 2014; Hautus et al., 2021).

claim: Detecting an oriented grating in noise can be achieved with a simple, local visual cortex computation: first, by aggregating responses of orientation-tuned visual neurons and then, by testing if this activity exceeds a pre-set threshold (Parker and Newsome, 1998).
source: For example, detecting an oriented grating in noise can be achieved with a simple, local visual cortex computation: first, by aggregating responses of orientation-tuned visual neurons and then, by testing if this activity exceeds a pre-set threshold (Parker and Newsome, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and established knowledge.

claim: Discriminating the orientation of a target grating involves an arguably more nuanced computation that requires comparing the relative activities of neurons tuned to different orientations relative to some predefined axis (Parker and Newsome, 1998).
source: By contrast, discriminating the orientation of a target grating involves an arguably more nuanced computation; one that requires comparing the relative activities of neurons tuned to different orientations relative to some predefined axis (e.g. vertical meridian; Parker and Newsome, 1998).

claim: Orientation discrimination computation would involve higher cortical areas for maintaining the feature discrimination rule in working memory, such as the prefrontal cortex (Funahashi, 2017; Zhang et al., 2023; Dupont et al., 1998).

claim: Detection and discrimination computations could be affected by attention differently (Maunsell, 2015).

claim: Conventional attentional blink task designs often conflate detection and discrimination computations.
source: This second question is particularly important because conventional attentional blink task designs often conflate these computations.

claim: An identification deficit during the attentional blink could arise from at least one of two sources: a detection deficit or a discrimination deficit (Raymond et al., 1992; Nieuwenstein et al., 2009; Chun and Potter, 1995; Vogel and Luck, 2002; Gross et al., 2004).
